questions.q: State the three levels of processing in Craik and Lockhart's theory in order from shallowest to deepest.
questions.a: Structural (physical features) → Phonemic (sound) → Semantic (meaning). A wrong answer that reverses the order or substitutes "acoustic" for "phonemic" reveals the student has memorised labels without understanding the depth hierarchy; they may think deeper processing means "more complex sound analysis" rather than meaning extraction.

questions.q: Explain why elaborative rehearsal leads to better long-term retention than maintenance rehearsal, using the concept of processing depth.
questions.a: Maintenance rehearsal (e.g., rote repetition) keeps information at structural/phonemic levels—shallow processing—so the trace is fragile. Elaborative rehearsal connects new information to existing semantic networks, forcing deep processing; the richer associative network creates multiple retrieval paths, making the memory more durable. A wrong answer that says "elaborative rehearsal takes more time" confuses effort with depth; time alone does not guarantee semantic encoding.

questions.q: A teacher asks students to learn the word "photosynthesis". Group A counts the syllables; Group B writes a sentence using the word; Group C draws the chemical equation. Predict the recall order from best to worst after 24 hours and justify using levels of processing.
questions.a: Best: Group C (semantic – drawing the equation requires understanding meaning), then Group B (semantic – sentence generation requires meaning), worst: Group A (phonemic – syllable counting is sound-based). If a student ranks Group B above Group C, they may not recognise that generating a sentence can sometimes stay at a shallow syntactic level, whereas drawing a biochemical equation forces deeper conceptual integration.

questions.q: Compare the Stage Model's view of rehearsal (maintenance vs. elaborative) with the Levels of Processing view. Identify one key similarity and one key difference.
questions.a: Similarity: Both distinguish shallow (maintenance/structural-phonemic) from deep (elaborative/semantic) rehearsal. Difference: Stage Model treats rehearsal as a control process that moves information *into* LTM; Levels of Processing argues rehearsal *type* determines trace durability *within* a single memory system—there is no separate STM/LTM structural boundary. A wrong answer that says "they are the same theory" misses the fundamental architectural disagreement.

questions.q: Critique the claim: "To maximise memory, always use semantic encoding." Provide two limitations of this advice based on the theory or subsequent research.
questions.a: 1) Transfer-appropriate processing: If the test requires rhyme recognition (phonemic), semantic encoding may not help as much as phonemic encoding. 2) Cognitive load: Deep processing demands more attentional resources; under divided attention, shallow processing may be the only feasible option. A student who says "semantic is always best" ignores context-dependency and resource constraints, showing an overgeneralised understanding.

questions.q: Design a 5-minute classroom activity that forces semantic encoding of the term "cognitive dissonance" for Class 11 students. Specify the task, the processing level targeted, and how you would verify depth.
questions.a: Task: "Write a real-life dilemma where you experienced cognitive dissonance, explain the conflicting cognitions, and describe how you resolved it." Target: Semantic (personal meaning, elaboration). Verification: Collect responses; check for accurate use of "conflicting beliefs/behaviours" and "resolution strategy" – not just dictionary definition. A poor activity would be "memorise the definition" (shallow) or "list synonyms" (phonemic/structural).
